<reflection>
All mechanisms fit the baseline run nearly equally well (NLL ~ -18.56), except M5 which is notably worse. This is expected: a single run with moderate conditions is not very discriminating. Almost all mechanisms can reproduce a simple Michaelis-Menten-like trace.

To discriminate, I need to probe regions where the mechanisms diverge:
- High catalyst concentration: tests dimerization (M2, M3, M13) and catalyst-catalyst deactivation (M13, M19)
- High substrate concentration: tests substrate inhibition (M11, M16) and substrate-coupled deactivation
- Added product: tests product inhibition (M12, M17)
- Low catalyst with long time: tests deactivation (M9, M14, M20)

My aim for the turn (establish baseline) was achieved, but discrimination power is minimal.
</reflection>

<hypothesis>
I'll propose a high-catalyst experiment. This tests:
- Mechanisms with catalyst dimerization: M2, M3 (productive dimer) vs M13 (deactivating dimer) — catalyst dimerization is concentration-squared dependent, so high [cat] amplifies differences.
- Mechanisms with bimolecular cat/catS deactivation: M19
- Also provides stronger signal on turnover rate vs. catalyst loading (linear for M1, M4-M8, M9-M12, M14-M18; nonlinear for M2, M3, M13, M19)
- Helps separate M4 (X + catS pathway) since X might be generated in proportion to cat

Using cat = 0.1 M (10× baseline) with moderate S = 1.0 and no product gives a strong test of catalyst-order dependence.
</hypothesis>
